title: A lead's score lands exactly on a tier line
when: A lead's score is exactly on the line between two tiers (for example exactly the warm threshold).
steps: Agent 02 (Lead Qualification) gives the lead the lower tier.
It tells you the score sat on a tier line and the lower tier was given, so you can look at it.
never: Round a borderline lead up into the higher tier.
why: Treating a borderline lead as hotter than it is can mean pressure contact the person did not invite. You decide whether to move it up.
you_see: A question saying the score is on a tier line, with the score and the tier given.
test: Your signed rubric: budget over $400,000 scores 40, a timeline under 30 days scores 40, pre-approval scores 20; warm starts at 40. A lead with a $450,000 budget, a 90-day timeline and no financing scores exactly 40 and is recorded cold.

title: There is no signed scoring rubric
when: A lead arrives to be scored and no signed rubric is in force (none was ever signed, or it cannot be read).
steps: Agent 02 does not score the lead.
It tells you scoring is stopped because no rubric is active.
No alert about the lead is raised.
never: Score from a remembered or default rubric.
why: Scores decide who you call first. A score from a rubric you did not sign is a guess with your name on it.
you_see: A question saying no rubric is active.
test: The system starts without the signed rubric; a lead with a $500,000 budget and a 10-day timeline comes in.

title: A lead demands a person: straight to the hot path
when: A lead demands to speak to a person.
steps: Agent 02 treats the lead as hot whatever its score, so you are alerted at once.
never: Let a low score bury a person who asked for a human.
why: Someone who asked for a person must get one quickly, whatever the numbers say.
you_see: Today the demand reaches you from Agent 01 directly (see LA-T-01-03).

title: A lead says it is urgent but shows no financing
when: A lead says the purchase is urgent but has made no progress on financing.
steps: Agent 02 scores on what can be checked (financing), not on the stated urgency.
It writes the conflict in the client's history, in plain words: stated urgency "high" conflicts with no financing progress.
never: Raise a score because someone says they are in a hurry.
why: Stated urgency costs nothing to say; financing shows real readiness. Scores built on what can be verified rank leads fairly.
you_see: The conflict in the lead's history next to its score.
test: A lead with "high" urgency, no financing, a $450,000 budget and a 60-day timeline. (Its score also lands exactly on the warm line, so it is recorded cold and you are asked, as in LA-T-02-01.)

title: A lead's tier keeps swinging
when: A lead's tier changes direction for the third time (for example hot, then cold, then hot).
steps: Agent 02 scores each inquiry as it comes.
On the third swing it asks you to review the lead: the swinging itself is the signal.
never: Treat repeated swings as noise and keep re-tiering silently.
why: A lead whose facts keep changing may be confused, testing you, or two people on one record. A person should look.
you_see: A question saying the lead's tier swung a third time, with its tier history.
test: Three inquiries on one client: a $500,000 budget, 10 days and pre-approval (hot); then $300,000, 90 days, no financing (cold); then hot again. The third also raises a hot-lead alert.

title: A signed rubric tries to change a fixed rule
when: A rubric you sign contains settings beyond the scoring weights (for example a weight for "demands a human", which is a fixed rule, not a score).
steps: Agent 02 uses only the scoring settings it is allowed to read; the fixed rule stands.
The extra settings are never read.
It tells you which settings it ignored, so the rubric can be corrected.
never: Let a rubric quietly override a fixed rule, or quietly drop what it tried.
why: Fixed rules (a person asking for a human, consent) are not up for scoring. A rubric that tries to change one is a mistake you should see.
you_see: A question naming the rubric settings that were ignored.
test: A signed rubric version "t-extra" with the usual weights plus "demands_human_weight": 0.

title: A lead's pre-approval letter has expired
when: A lead provides a pre-approval letter that has expired.
steps: Agent 02 scores the lead as having no verified financing.
It notes in the client's history that the pre-approval letter expired.
never: Count an expired letter as financing.
why: An expired letter proves nothing about today's buying power; counting it would put the lead ahead of others unfairly.
you_see: The note "pre-approval letter expired" with the lead's score.
test: A lead with a $500,000 budget, a 20-day timeline and an expired $500,000 pre-approval letter scores 80: budget and timeline only, no financing points.

title: The "lead" is another agent shopping for a client
when: The inquiry comes from a real estate agent looking on behalf of their client.
steps: Agent 02 does not score it as a consumer lead.
It flags it as agent-to-agent and asks you how to engage.
never: Put another agent into your consumer lead process.
why: Agent-to-agent business has its own rules and etiquette; treating it as a consumer lead would send the wrong messages.
you_see: A question saying this is an agent-to-agent inquiry.
test: An inquiry flagged as an agent shopping for a client, with a $700,000 budget, 10 days and pre-approval (hot if scored).

title: An unsigned rubric change arrives
when: A change to the scoring rubric arrives without your signature.
steps: The dispatcher refuses it; Agent 02 never receives it.
You are alerted to an integrity problem.
Scoring carries on with the last rubric you signed.
never: Adopt a scoring change you did not sign.
why: Whoever controls the rubric controls who gets called. Only you may change it.
you_see: An integrity alert; scores keep using your signed rubric version.
test: An unsigned rubric that would make a $100 budget count as high arrives. A lead with a $300,000 budget and a 90-day timeline then scores cold on your signed rubric "synth-v1".

title: A lead's stated budget is higher than their pre-approval
when: The budget a lead states is higher than the amount on their pre-approval document.
steps: Agent 02 scores on the document's amount.
It writes the conflict in the client's history word for word.
never: Score on the stated budget when a document says otherwise.
why: The document is evidence; the stated number is a wish. Scoring on evidence keeps the ranking honest.
you_see: The conflict noted with the lead's score.
test: A lead says $600,000 but the pre-approval is for $350,000. The score is 60 (timeline and financing, no budget points) and the lead goes to follow-up as warm.

title: A re-score arrives while you are handling a hot lead
when: A lead is hot and its alert is still open with you, and a re-score request arrives.
steps: Agent 02 does not re-score it.
It holds the request and tells you a re-score arrived during an open alert.
never: Change a lead's tier while you are working it.
why: Your read of a lead you are talking to outranks a formula. Re-tiering mid-conversation could pull it out from under you.
you_see: A question saying a re-score came in during the open alert.
test: A hot lead raises an alert. A re-score request with lower numbers then arrives. Stand-in: Agent 03 only re-scores warm leads, so the test sends it as Agent 03.

title: Nothing is known about a lead's budget, timeline or financing
when: A lead gives none of the facts the rubric uses.
steps: Agent 02 records the tier as UNKNOWN, not cold.
It stops scoring the lead and asks you.
never: Treat missing facts as a low score.
why: Unknown is not cold. Archiving a lead because they did not fill in the form loses real buyers.
you_see: A question saying all scoring inputs are unknown; the lead's tier shows UNKNOWN.
test: A web form with only a name and an email.

title: The scoring engine is not confident enough
when: The decision engine scores a lead but reports a confidence below the floor you signed.
steps: Agent 02 does not act on the uncertain tier; it holds the lead and asks you to continue or cancel.
Continue: the lead is scored with your signed rubric and acted on (for example a hot-lead alert).
Cancel: the lead is archived and nothing is sent.
never: Act on a tier the engine itself is unsure of.
why: An uncertain score can send a lead down the wrong path. You decide whether to trust your rubric instead.
you_see: A held lead asking you to continue or cancel, naming the confidence and the floor.
test: You sign a confidence floor of 0.9. The engine scores a lead at confidence 0.85. You continue: the signed rubric scores it hot and you get a hot-lead alert.

title: Lead data would go to the outside scoring service
when: The outside decision engine could be used to score a lead.
steps: Lead data goes to the outside service only when both are true: a service key is installed AND you have signed "allow external".
Otherwise nothing is sent out and the local engine scores the lead.
never: Send lead data out because a key happens to be installed.
why: Personal data leaving your office is your decision, and it must be a signed one.
you_see: The lead's score; the record shows the local engine made it.
test: You sign "allow external" but no key is installed. A lead comes in: nothing is sent out and the local engine scores it.

title: The scoring engine returns a tier nobody knows
when: The decision engine returns a tier name Agent 02 does not recognize.
steps: Agent 02 treats it as below the confidence floor.
It holds the lead and asks you to continue or cancel, as in LA-T-02-13.
never: Act on, or guess the meaning of, an unknown tier.
why: An unrecognized answer is not an answer. Holding is the safe default.
you_see: A held lead asking you to continue or cancel.

title: A warm lead goes to follow-up with its scoring facts
when: A lead scores warm and is passed to Agent 03 (Lead Nurture) for follow-up.
steps: Agent 02 sends the lead's scoring facts along (budget, timeline, financing).
Agent 03 uses them to re-score the lead on its schedule.
never: Pass a warm lead on without the facts needed to re-score it.
why: Without the original facts, a later re-score would have to guess. With them, it counts the timeline down honestly.
you_see: Nothing extra; the lead starts its follow-up sequence.
test: A lead with a $500,000 budget, a 60-day timeline and pre-approval scores warm and goes to follow-up.
